newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Thousands of South Africans seek apartheid amnesty.
newsitem.headline: Thousands of South Africans seek apartheid amnesty.

text.p: South Africa's truth commission fielded a last-minute flurry of amnesty applications on Friday, 24 hours before the deadline, but said some groups involved in apartheid crime and violence had failed to come forward.

Officials of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission told reporters about 6,300 people had applied for indemnity from prosecution or civil damages claims, more than 500 of them over the last week, as the Saturday midnight deadline loomed.
But they said no members of the former white-led defence force had applied and fewer than 100 members of the Zulu-based Inkatha Freedom Party had come forward.
Inkatha fought a decade-long turf war with the African National Congress in which about 15,000 people were killed. The feud erupted more than a decade ago and is still simmering.
"They are missing out on a wonderful opportunity to bring the curtain down on this horrendous period of history," truth commission chairman Archbishop Desmond Tutu said.

Commission sources said that in the last week three high-profile ANC politicians had applied for amnesty. The commission refuses to give names of applicants, but many politicians have gone on record on whether they plan to apply.
ANC Defence Minister Joe Modise said he would apply but his apartheid predecessor, General Magnus Malan, said he would not.
The commission, mandated to grant amnesty to those who make full confessions, warned Malan on Friday that he could be making a mistake.
"He would be well advised not only in terms of reconciliation but in terms of his own self-interest to apply for amnesty even at this 11th hour," commission deputy chairman Alex Boraine said.
The only two surviving former white presidents, P.W. Botha and F.W. de Klerk, have also said they saw no reason to apply for amnesty because they committed no crime.
Most of the leadership of the African National Congress, with the likely exception of President Nelson Mandela, were expected to file amnesty applications.
Malan testified voluntarily to the commission on Wednesday, saying he accepted moral responsibility for the actions of the defence force, including raids on ANC targets in neighbouring countries.

"However, I do not intend to seek amnesty for those operations," he said. "If with the wisdom of hindsight...my authority should be regarded by some as culpable, I am prepared to face the consequences."

The deadline for amnesty applications was originally December last year, but Mandela extended it by five months at the request of commission chairman Archbishop Desmond Tutu because relatively few people had lodged applications.

The commission, set up in 1995 to uncover as much as possible about political crimes and human rights abuses during the apartheid era, hopes the lure of amnesty will persuade perpetrators to reveal their secrets.
Dozens of former security police officers have applied, including those responsible for the death of black activist Steve Biko in 1977.
Political analyst Laurie Nathan said it was significant that Malan had accepted moral responsibility, but added that only if he applied for amnesty would the full story of his activities be told.
"I think that he may be experiencing pressure from other soldiers," Nathan said.
"Senior members of the old defence force feel betrayed that their political and military leadership have denied responsibility or claimed ignorance. And these soldiers were operating under orders."
